question: In children with asthma, a long-acting beta-2 agonist (LABA) such as salmeterol may be used as monotherapy (without an inhaled corticosteroid) when symptoms are not adequately controlled on a short-acting bronchodilator alone.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false — a critical safety point. LABAs must NEVER be used as monotherapy in children with asthma. They are step-up add-on therapy combined with ICS (GINA Step 3+). Using LABA alone suppresses bronchoconstriction without controlling underlying inflammation, risking progressive, undetected airway damage and potentially fatal exacerbations. Always pair a LABA with an ICS.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. LABA monotherapy in asthma is contraindicated in children (and adults). LABAs lack anti-inflammatory action and, when used alone, can mask worsening airway inflammation while providing symptomatic bronchodilation. This combination has been associated with increased risk of severe exacerbations and asthma-related death. GINA guidelines mandate that LABAs must always be co-prescribed with an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) — either as separate inhalers or a fixed-dose ICS/LABA combination.
